title: Hi, how are you?
goal: Greet Brazilians the right way at any time of day, say your name and where you're from, ask how someone is, and discover that Portuguese questions keep normal word order — no *do you* needed.
bekal: greet people with *oi*, *bom dia*, *boa tarde* and *boa noite*, each at the right time
say your name and origin with *eu sou…* and *eu sou de…*
ask a question just by raising your voice, without changing the word order

notes: **Tudo bem? is a greeting, not a real question.** Literally "all good?", and the answer is almost always *tudo bem* too — even when your life is falling apart. It works exactly like "how's it going?" in English: an opening ritual, not a request for a report. You can answer *tudo bem*, *tudo bom* or *tudo ótimo*, and all three are correct.

**Look at Carla's question: the word order doesn't change.** *Você é brasileira?* has exactly the same word order as *Você é brasileira.* The only difference is the voice rising at the end — just like a casual "You're Brazilian?" in English. No helper word to add (no *do*, no *are you*), nothing to flip around. This is Portuguese's first gift to you.

**Answering "yes" by repeating the verb.** Look at Carla's answer: not just *sim*, but *Sou, sim*. Brazilians very often answer yes/no questions by repeating the verb of the question: *Você é brasileira?* → *Sou.* Answering with just *sim* isn't wrong, but repeating the verb sounds far more natural.

**Eu me chamo is literally "I call myself".** There's a little word *me* in the middle, like *myself*. Simpler forms exist and are just as correct: *Meu nome é Budi* ("my name is Budi") or even *Eu sou o Budi*.

grammars.title: Ser — the first verb "to be"
body: The first verb you absolutely need to master, and also the most irregular. Don't look for a pattern; learn its six lines like a song.
after: **Você uses the same form as "he/she".** Look at rows two and three: *você é* and *ele é* — the verb form is identical. Brazilian Portuguese uses *você* for everyone, casual or polite, and that cuts your memorizing in half. Old grammar books teach *tu falas*; in ninety percent of Brazil, that form isn't used.

**The subject pronoun can be dropped.** *Sou de Jacarta* can only mean "I'm from Jakarta", because only "I" uses the form *sou*. Brazilians drop it all the time. Use *eu* when you want to **stress** it: *Eu sou indonésio, ela é brasileira*.
⚠️ There's a second verb "to be", *estar*, used for temporary things. It gets a whole unit to itself in unit 3. For now, use *ser* for name, origin and nationality — and you'll always be right.

grammars.title: Subject pronouns
body: Six forms to memorize, plus two you only need to recognize.
after: **Portuguese has a separate "they" for men and for women.** *Eles* for a group of men (or a mixed group), *elas* for a group of women only. English has one *they*; Portuguese makes you choose, and it will be one of the mistakes you make most often at first.

**A gente is the biggest secret of spoken Brazilian Portuguese.** Literally "the people", but it means "we" — and it takes the **third-person singular** verb form, just like *ele*: *A gente é brasileiro*, not *a gente somos*. In everyday conversation you'll hear *a gente* far more often than *nós*. Good news for you: using it means one fewer verb form to memorize.

blocks.text: ⚠️ *Obrigado* changes according to **who says it**, not who receives it. Men always say *obrigado*; women always say *obrigada* — even to other women. It's the most common mistake foreigners make in Brazil, and the easiest to fix.

The last two phrases in that table are worth more than a hundred memorized words. *Fala mais devagar* keeps a conversation going when it's run away from you, and *Como se diz…?* turns every Brazilian around you into a walking dictionary.
Portuguese sorts greetings by the clock, not by level of politeness. This table covers them all.

rows: Good evening / good night — arriving or leaving

blocks.text: ⚠️ *Boa noite* works **both ways** — to greet people when you walk into a room at night, and to say goodbye before bed. Portuguese doesn't split them the way English splits *good evening* and *good night*.

Notice, too, that *bom* goes with *dia* but *boa* with *tarde* and *noite*. That's no accident: *dia* is a masculine word, while *tarde* and *noite* are feminine. The full rule comes in unit 2 — for now, learn the three greetings as single chunks.
